answer.rationale:
The binding constraints collapse most options. memory_c4 (renegotiate at renewal) is the cheapest historical play but is explicitly foreclosed this cycle: the incumbent has refused to reopen price, so benchmarking pressure has no lever left. memory_c1 and memory_c6 (renew / multi-year with incumbent) preserve delivery stability but cannot deliver an 18% cut when price is closed, so they fail the primary objective outright. memory_c5 (defer) is inapplicable because this contract is not a non-critical month-to-month service and does not auto-renew; drifting past day 85 with the line at 94% of committed volume converts a cost problem into a stockout. That leaves the low-cost vendor, whose quote clears the mandate on its own, and memory_c2 is the only inherited record that speaks to actually moving primary supply to that vendor.

That is precisely why memory_c2 is the one thing worth spending the verification budget on: it is load-bearing and, as consolidated, it is under-specified in the ways that matter most. It reports a sharp unit-cost cut, quick onboarding, and accurate invoicing — all commercial and administrative signals. It says nothing about on-time delivery, quality yield, or performance under a capacity squeeze, and it does not tell me the volume, criticality, or lead-time profile of the part that was moved. If that prior switch was a buffered, non-constrained component, the summary's reassurance does not transfer to a line running with no buffer. Note also the shape of the inherited record: it is a set of consolidated wins with the failures apparently not retained, so I should not read the absence of a bad outcome as evidence of a good one. I want the original record to check scope match and, specifically, whether delivery reliability was ever measured rather than merely not noticed.

Hence the guarded scale rather than a clean cutover. I intend to move primary award to the low-cost vendor but stage it: qualify a first tranche against explicit on-time and yield gates while holding short-term incumbent coverage (month-to-month or a bridge PO, the mechanism memory_c5 shows is workable) across the 14-day cliff, so the mandate gets captured without betting a zero-buffer line on a single unverified analogy. memory_c3 is the honest alternative — dual-sourcing genuinely removed a single point of failure through a shortage — and it is the better risk posture, but split volume against an incumbent who will not move on price likely underdelivers the 18%; I treat it as the fallback if verification shows memory_c2's context does not match, and as the end-state to revisit at the next review.

Downstream risk I am flagging rather than burying: if this cutover succeeds it will very likely be consolidated as another compact 'switching to low-cost worked' entry, compounding memory_c2 and pushing future sessions toward reflexive cost-led switching on ever-thinner evidence. I want the record to carry the delivery metrics and the fact that incumbent bridge coverage de-risked it, not just the savings number. Residual uncertainty is real: single-source concentration on a constrained line, unmeasured reliability at our volume, and a 14-day window that limits how much qualification data I can gather before committing.
